xni7.github.io/gst

Do not read the title or the pkgdown link. The accepted program title remains: Totality of Evidence in Minutes: Interactive Apps for GST Power and Publication-Ready Forest Plot. Move to slide 2 for the problem.

The two headaches

The design headache

Several endpoints, correlated, with different effect sizes. Power depends on all of them — and on the test.

The reporting headache

Every change to a header or an interval colour means another round of plotting code. 

p <- forest_data() |>
  forest_plot(
    ci_color = "#008A99",
    display_cols = c(
      "Group", "forest",
      "est+ci", "p"))
# edit, re-run, re-export

The solution: {gst} provides two interactive apps that connect analytical trial planning with reproducible reporting.

Speak the problem here: several endpoints, how to assess the evidence overall and communicate it. Then advance to the arc. The code on the right is illustrative, not an exported script.

The two apps

GST Power App (Plan it · Power it)
  • Size studies analytically from effects and correlations.
  • See when combining endpoints helps or hurts.
  • No repeated-trial simulation script for each scenario.
Forest Plot App (Publish it)
  • Flexible journal-style formatting.
  • No patient-level data (summary statistics only).
  • Export figures, data and R code to rebuild the plot.

Model-based analytical calculations support exploration. Simulation can still assess calibration.

The path is plan it, power it, publish it. The Power App explores GST power and sample size analytically, without a repeated-trial simulation for each scenario. The Forest Plot App reports endpoint summaries as a journal-style figure, with R code to reproduce it.

Methods in {gst}

What is a GST?
A global statistical test assesses a joint signal across endpoints.Note: a significant global test does not mean every endpoint improved.
The weights
Equal-weight OLS or inverse-correlation GLS (O’Brien, 1984).
The cutoff
Degrees-of-freedom approximations: Dallow, O’Brien, Logan–Tamhane.
O’Brien Plus (GST_Any)
Power for the joint test and at least one individual endpoint being significant.

Also in {gst}: Wei–Lachin; gst::obt(), an O’Brien-based truncated closed-testing routine (Luo et al., 2025) — not in today’s demos. DOI: 10.1002/pst.70010

OLS and GLS are two weighting choices for the O’Brien test; Dallow, O’Brien, and Logan & Tamhane are degrees-of-freedom approximations for the t-cutoff, not extra tests. obt() is a package routine, not a control in either Shiny demo. O’Brien Plus is reported as GST_Any in the Power App table. Leave Wei–Lachin and obt() unspoken.

Full citation: Luo X, Li L, Savenkov O, Liu W, Ni X, Tang W, Guo W. Multiple Comparisons Procedures for Analyses of Joint Primary Endpoints and Secondary Endpoints. Pharmaceutical Statistics. 2025;24(3):e70010. DOI: 10.1002/pst.70010.

Three designs, different power

Design Effects (δ₁, δ₂) Correlation ρ OES GST power Best individual
Balanced (0.4, 0.4) 0.3 0.50 94% 80%
Redundant (0.4, 0.4) 0.9 0.41 82% 80%
Uneven (0.5, 0.1) 0.8 0.32 60% 94%
A weak endpoint highly correlated with a strong one costs you power. Settle that before the data arrive.

Two endpoints, n = 100 per arm, two-sided α = .05, O’Brien OLS, Dallow df = 198. OES from gst::get_oes(); GST power is two-sample t power at the OES. Rounded as in the app; bold marks the higher power in each row. Best individual is a planning benchmark, not a multiplicity-adjusted selection rule.

Recording slide, right after the live Power App (about 15 s), then advance to the OES slide. Narrate patterns, not exact powers. Balanced: GST beats the strongest individual endpoint. Redundant: much smaller advantage. Uneven: GST falls below the strong endpoint alone.

Operational effect size (OES)

For equal-weight OLS, at the same n and degrees of freedom, the global test beats the best single endpoint when OES exceeds the largest single effect.

O’Brien OLS operational effect size, gst::get_oes(): 1ᵀδ / √(1ᵀR1). The three designs: 0.50 vs 0.40, 0.41 vs 0.40, 0.32 vs 0.50. A planning comparison, not permission to pick the test after seeing the data.

Recording slide (about 15 s). Equal-weight OLS reduces each design to one operational effect size. For these rows, at the same n and df, GST wins when OES exceeds the largest single effect. Planning only.

Sizing the study

Single endpoint
Effect 0.4 → about 100 per arm for 80% power.
GST, balanced design
Effects (0.4, 0.4), ρ = 0.3 → 65 per arm for 80% power.

✓ Calculated analytically with noncentral t distributions — no simulation grid needed to explore.

Widget screenshot from the gst vignette: a different example — effects (0.5, 0.5), ρ = 0.5 → 49 per arm.

65 per arm from gst::get_n() in gst 0.3.1 (power 80.2%); single endpoint 80.4% at n = 100 (pwr::pwr.t2n.test). Two-sided α = .05, Dallow df.

Backup slide. The live Sample Size Calculation tab is the recording path. Do not attach the screenshot’s 49 / 0.577 / 0.807 to the n = 100 designs. Do not enter a correlation above 1 on this widget.

Combining can help or dilute

Correlation-adjusted Stouffer
Case (p₁, p₂) ρ Combined p
1 · Helps (.08, .08) .3 .0261
2 · Misses .05 (.08, .08) .9 .0627
3 · Dilutes best (.00051, .48) .8 .0259
1 → 2: the point did not move; the .05 boundary did. Case 2 is still below .08.
3: below .05, but weaker than its best single p (.00051).

Hypothetical p-values; separate from O’Brien power. gst’s Stouffer: one-sided z, Nyholt effective-test scaling (gst:::p_combine). Curves: combined p = .05 boundaries. Shaded: case 1 gain. Axes use sqrt(p) spacing.

Each curve marks the 0.05 cutoff for the combined p-value. That comparison is for understanding dilution, not a rule for picking the test after the data are in. Do not use the older contour that prints joint p = 0.039, 0.041, and 0.075.

The forest plot

Input

Summary statistics (estimate, CI, p) via table, paste or CSV template. No patient-level data.

Formatting

Edit CI colours, column widths and headers interactively.

Transformations

Invert reverses the plotted direction; printed numbers stay as entered.

Standardize shows standard-error units; printed estimates and nominal p-values unchanged.

Built-in demo values from {gst}, not clinical results. Starred row: plotted direction reversed; printed estimate unchanged. Review against target-journal requirements.

Backup for the live Forest Plot App. Invert reverses the plotted direction; the printed numbers stay as entered. Standardize Plot shows estimates and intervals in standard-error units; printed estimates stay on the original scale and p-values stay nominal.

From the app to R

Interactive edits (the app)

In the app

R Code Save Code Copy

Exports

CSV / RDS for data · PNG / JPEG for figures

Reproducible R (the script) 
library(gst)
p <- forest_data() |>
  forest_plot(
    ci_color = "#008A99",
    ci_color_inverted = "#C44B49",
    display_cols = c(
      "Group", "forest", "est+ci", "p"))
writeLines(forest_reprex(p),
           "forest-reproduce.R")
The app gives the code and the data to rebuild the plot outside the interface. We still review output against journal requirements — but we don’t rebuild every revision by hand.

Compact workflow shown. The companion export rpharma-forest-example.R (gst 0.3.1) reproduces forest-plot.png; slide 9 shows a display copy of it.

Backup for the live Forest Plot App. Open the R Code panel rather than only hovering over the button.
